item_manifest_row.title: A countable discrete measurable space is standard Borel
item_manifest_row.statement: If S is nonempty and at most countable, then (S,P(S)) is standard Borel.
item_manifest_row.strategy: Use the discrete metric: it is complete and induces the power-set Borel sigma-algebra, while S itself is an at most countable dense subset.

references.title: David Marker, Descriptive Set Theory, Example 1.2, course notes (Fall 2002)
references.locator: §1, Example 1.2, PDF p. 2: the discrete metric on a countable set is complete and induces the discrete topology.

citations.quote: - $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$. - $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$. - $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite. - $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets $\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions: whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function $d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$: - **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$. - **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$. - **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset $F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is open.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.
Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The **Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

e u$ holds, so $d(s,u)=1\le d(s,t)+d(t,u)$; if $s=u$, the triangle inequality follows from nonnegativity. Thus [F3] makes $d$ a metric. For every $s\in S$, [F4] gives $B(s,1/2)=\{s\}$, so [F5] shows that every subset of $S$ is open.

If $(s_n)$ is Cauchy, [F6] with the rational $\epsilon=1/2$ gives an index $N$ such that $d(s_m,s_n)<1/2$ for all $m,n\ge N$. Hence all $s_n$ for $n\ge N$ are equal, so the sequence converges in $S$; by [F7], $d$ is complete. Since $S$ is at-most-countable and dense in itself, [F8] makes $(S,d)$ separable.

The power set is closed under relative complements and countable unions, so it is a sigma-algebra by [F2]. By [F10] and step 1.1, every subset of $S$ belongs to the Borel sigma-algebra. Conversely, every Borel set is a subset of $S$, so this sigma-algebra is exactly $\mathcal P(S)$. Therefore $(S,d)$ is Polish by [F9], and the identity map from $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ to $(S,\mathcal B(S,d))$ is a measurable bijection with measurable inverse.
The identity map in step 3.1 is a measurable isomorphism to a Polish space, so [F11] gives that $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ is standard Borel.

finite_checks.name: singleton discrete metric
finite_checks.calculation: The only metric value is d(s,s)=0; B(s,1/2)={s}; every sequence in the singleton is constant and converges.
